titleStmt.title: On Inventions; or, Fragments and Testimonia

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un helleniste) a partir du grec du corpus zoomathia sous zoo50/1g (Straton de Lampsaque, receuil de fragments et temoignages, source DFHG Project). Ce texte n'est pas une oeuvre continue mais un recueil savant de type critique (a la maniere de l'edition Wehrli des fragments de Straton) : chaque division de premier niveau (type "book"/"chapter"/"section", numerotation qui se repete/reinitialise d'un fragment a l'autre -- il ne s'agit pas d'une hierarchie d'oeuvre reelle mais du systeme de numerotation des fragments) correspond a un temoignage independant, combinant souvent une citation de source (auteur, oeuvre, page chez un editeur moderne) et le texte grec cite. Le contenu porte tres majoritairement sur la physique et la psychologie peripateticiennes de Straton (vide, lieu, poids, elements, perception, memoire, ame, sommeil, reves) plutot que sur la zoologie au sens strict -- Straton est present dans le corpus en tant que philosophe de la nature ayant notamment redige des traites aujourd'hui perdus "Sur les animaux embarrassants" et "Sur les animaux legendaires" (cf. fr. 1, catalogue de Diogene Laerce), et le dernier fragment (48) est lui-meme un temoignage sur son traite Περὶ εὑρημάτων (Sur les inventions), qui donne son titre au recueil. Les references de sources (noms d'auteurs anciens, titres d'oeuvres, noms d'editeurs modernes, pages/lignes) sont conservees telles quelles ; seul le grec et la prose de liaison ont ete traduits. Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un helleniste avant toute citation savante. Correspond au texte grec deja present dans le corpus sous zoo50/1g.

div.p: Fragments. 1. Straton, Philosopher.

Diogenes Laertius V 59: the following books of his (i.e. Strato's) are in circulation: 1. On Kingship, three books; 2. On Justice, three books; 3. On the Good, three books; 4. On the Gods, three books; 5. On First Principles, three or two books; 6. On Ways of Life; 7. On Happiness; 8. On Kingship; 9. On Philosophy; 10. On Courage; 11. On the Void; 12. On the Heaven; 13. On Breath (Pneuma); 14. On Human Nature; 15. On the Generation of Living Things; 16. On Mixture; 17. On Sleep; 18. On Dreams; 19. On Vision; 20. On Sensation; 21. On Pleasure; 22. On Colours; 23. On Diseases; 24. On Critical Days (or Judgements); 25. On Powers (or Faculties); 26. On Metals; 27. Mechanics; 28. On Dizziness and Fits of Darkening; 29. On the Light and the Heavy; 30. On Divine Possession (Enthusiasm); 31. On Time; 32. On Nourishment and Growth; 33. On Puzzling Animals; 34. On Legendary Animals; 35. On Causes; 36. Solutions to Difficulties; 37. Prefaces on Commonplaces (Topics); 38. On Accident; 39. On Definition; 40. On the More and the Less; 41. On the Unjust; 42. On the Prior and the Posterior; 43. On the Prior Genus; 44. On the Proprium (What Is One's Own); 45. On the Future; 46. Two Books of Refutations of Discoveries; 47. Disputed Notes; 48. Letters, of which the opening runs: 'Strato to Arsinoe, greetings.' [two further, unclear catalogue entries follow in the manuscript].

Plutarch, On the Contradictions of the Stoics XXIV, 1045f (SVF II, fr. 126): in the third book on dialectic, having said (namely Chrysippus) that Plato took dialectic seriously, and Aristotle, and those who came after them...

...down to Polemo and Strato, and Socrates most of all; and, having added that one might well be willing to err along with men so many and so great, he continues, quoting exactly: 'for if they had spoken of these matters only in passing, one might perhaps make light of the subject; but since they spoke of it with such care, as of something among the greatest and most necessary of faculties, it is not plausible that they were so entirely mistaken, being on the whole the kind of men we suppose them to be.' 'What then,' someone might say, 'do you yourself never cease fighting and refuting such great and numerous men, as you think, in the matters most authoritative and most important? For surely they did not write carefully about dialectic, but about first principle and end and the gods and justice only in passing and in jest — matters in which you call their reasoning blind, self-contradictory, and guilty of countless other errors.' Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's Categories, p. 423, 1ff Kalbfleisch (cf. Scholia on Aristotle's Categories, fr. 89a37 Brandis): 'and Strato of Lampsacus too, in his single book On the Prior and the Posterior, enumerated many modes, which I think can be reduced to the five modes stated here, being, as it were, a subdivision of them. For under the prior in time will be classed what is called the incomplete, in relation to the complete, since in all things the end comes last; and the same thing falls also under order. Further, under both of these, and also under the prior in worth, in power, and in nature, falls that of which...

...the knowledge is prior, as of the unit or the pair, and of plurality or of the even and the odd. For these do not convert with respect to the consequence of being, any more than the knowledge of them does. And a thing is prior both in time and in worth, of which the effect is prior, as the good is prior to the bad; for the one is a cause of preservation, the other of destruction, and being is prior to perishing both in time and in worth. And a thing is prior in nature when it does not convert with respect to the consequence of being — which can hold when the other of two things does not exist, as place is prior to body, and body to colour; and likewise if the one is naturally constituted within the other, as substance is prior to quality and quantity. So too what is according to nature is prior to what is against nature, and law to lawlessness, and possession (habit) to privation. Under the prior in worth and in power would also be classed those things more akin to what is more honourable, as quantity would be placed before quality...

...since quantity is part of substance, but quality is not. And if the one shares in coming-to-be and passing-away, as time does, and the other does not, as place does not; and if the one is separable, and the other not — for it is impossible for soul to exist without sensation, though it is possible for it to exist without desire. And the indivisible is prior to the divisible, since it is more like a first principle, as the centre is prior to the circle. And that which shares more fully in the prior is itself prior, as the eternal is prior to the good, the perishable to the bad, and the even to the pair, the odd to the triad. And if the one persists for some time and the other does not, as body persists more than motion and time. And under the prior in order would fall that of the intervening term which is prior, and the posterior that which is posterior. Under the prior as cause in convertible things would be the element, which is prior; for the part too is prior to the whole, as the finite is to the infinite, and if one thing comes from another, as bronze is prior to the statue, for this too is a material cause. And that the same thing can be prior and posterior in different respects, Strato himself showed, demonstrating that time and place are prior and posterior to one another.' Scholia on Aristotle's Categories, p. 89a37 Brandis: 'and so, since "prior" is said in many ways, he (namely Aristotle) makes the division without handing down all the modes — indeed he himself adds not a few others elsewhere, as does Strato too, in his single book On the Prior and the Posterior — thinking those he has set out sufficient for an introduction.' Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's Categories, p. 418, 24 Kalbfleisch: 'and so, since "prior" is said in many ways, he (namely Aristotle) makes the division, without handing down all the modes — indeed he himself adds not a few others elsewhere, as does Strato too, in his single book On the Prior and the Posterior — thinking those he has set out sufficient for an introduction.' Alexander of Aphrodisias, Commentary on Aristotle's Topics, p. 339, 30 Wallies: 'so then, when the convertible terms do not correspond in like manner, that which was posited as genus will be refuted. For if someone posits, as genus of the greater...

...the exceeding, since the terms convertible with these are not said with respect to like cases — for the lesser is lesser than something, namely than the greater, while the exceeded is exceeded by something, namely by that which exceeds — it would be refuted that the exceeding is the genus of the greater. Strato, however, adds to this topic yet another point: that if the terms themselves are said with respect to like cases — both the genus assigned and the species — but of the things to which these are related, one converts and the other does not, he says that what was posited will not be a genus. And he uses as an example of this topic deficiency and lack. For if someone calls lack a genus of deficiency, since each of them is assigned to the same case — for deficiency is deficiency of something, namely of excess, and lack likewise is lack of something, namely of the sufficient — but the two things to which each is related no longer convert with each other (for excess is itself of something, namely of deficiency, but the sufficient does not convert in this way, since the sufficient is not called 'sufficient for lack') — so lack would not be a genus of deficiency. But this man, wishing to innovate, actually destroys something greater by a small point; for it undermines the claim that all relative terms are said with respect to converting terms.' Plutarch, Against Colotes XIV, 1115b: 'and indeed, of the other Peripatetics, Strato, their foremost figure, agrees with Aristotle in many respects, yet holds views opposite to Plato's concerning motion, mind, soul, and generation; and, in the end, he says that the cosmos itself is not a living creature, and that what corresponds to nature follows what corresponds to chance; for spontaneity provides the starting-point...

...and only then are each of the natural processes brought to completion in this way. Maximus of Tyre XI 5e: 'they know it unwillingly and speak of it against their will (namely the divine); whether you strip it of goodness, as Leucippus does, or add like-feeling to it, as Democritus does, or alter its nature, as Strato does, or grant it pleasure, as Epicurus does, and so on.' Proclus, Commentary on Plato's Timaeus IV, 242f: 'so that it is not being, as Strato the natural philosopher says, that is the cause of persistence, but eternity — persistence not occurring perpetually, but existing unchangeably within a single instant, as Timaeus said.' Proclus, Commentary on Plato's Timaeus IV, 243b: 'eternity, however, is (the cause) of persistence within being. And Strato ought rather to have said this, instead of defining being as the persistence of existing things, as he wrote in his book On Being, transferring what is proper to eternity onto being.' Damascius, Doubts and Solutions, 62, I p. 135 Ruelle: 'for such is the power that remains within, of the kind that, once it has come forth toward the outside, becomes actuality; and such is substance, standing altogether still, of the kind that power is when it is preparing itself for motion. It was with this in view, it seems to me, that Strato too declared that being remains, since he saw that the extension of being was power. But he ought to have seen together that, even if remaining accompanies being, the two are nonetheless not the same, as our concepts clearly distinguish, recognizing being as one thing and remaining as another. For a thing must first exist, and only then remain or be in motion. And...

...remaining is opposed to being moved; for remaining and standing still are the same thing, whereas being has, as its opposite, either nothing, or else not-being, as Plato in many places sets it in opposition; so that if someone should define being also as subsistence, this notion comes to the same as Strato's; for 'subsisting' is itself a term related to standing still.' 41,2.1 Damascius, Doubts and Solutions, 63, I p. 138 Ruelle: 'for there is nothing opposed to actuality and to power, except substance, in some sense; substance, then, will be stability — this, I think, is Strato's point, which did not seem to be sound.' 42.1 Galen, History of Philosophy 18 (Diels, Doxographi Graeci p. 611): 'Strato, surnamed the natural philosopher, posits the qualities (namely as the principles of the universe).' 43.1 Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism III 33 (On the Material Principles): 'Strato the natural philosopher said the qualities (namely to be principles).' 45.1 Stobaeus, Eclogae I 10, 12 (Aetius I 3, 24, p. 288 Diels): Stobaeus — 'the elements are the hot and the cold.' 48.1 Epiphanius, Against Heresies III 33 (Diels, Doxographi Graeci p. 592): 'Strato of Lampsacus said that the hot substance was the cause of all things. He said the parts of the cosmos were infinite in number, and said that every living creature was capable of receiving mind.' 49.1 Plutarch, On the Primary Cold IX, 948c: 'nevertheless it is better to stir up beforehand these sensible qualities as well, in which Empedocles and Strato and the Stoics place the substances of the powers — the Stoics assigning the primarily cold to air, Empedocles and Strato to water...

...another might well appear to assign earth as cause of coldness instead.' Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's On the Heavens, p. 269, 4 Heiberg: 'it should be known that it was not Strato alone, nor Epicurus alone, who said that all bodies are heavy, and are borne downward by nature and upward against nature, but Plato too, and so on.' Stobaeus, Eclogae I 14, 1h (Aetius I 12, 7, p. 311 Diels): 'Strato (held) that a natural weight is present in bodies, and that the lighter float on the heavier, as though being pressed out from within them.' Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's On the Heavens, p. 267, 29 Heiberg: 'that the elements are not moved by being forced through mutual compression either, he (namely Aristotle) shows next. After him, Strato and Epicurus held this same opinion, thinking that every body has weight and is borne toward the centre, and that, as the heavier sink down, the less heavy are forced upward by them through violence — so that, if one were to remove the earth, water would come to the centre, and if the water, air, and if the air, fire.' Theodoret, Cure of the Greek Maladies IV 14: 'Strato, on the contrary, (says) that outside (the universe) there is nothing void, but that inside it is possible for there to be.' Stobaeus, Eclogae I 18, 1b (Aetius I 18, 4, p. 316 and I 19, 3, p. 317 Diels): 'Strato said that outside the cosmos there is no void, but that it is possible for it to occur within; and that place is the interval between the containing and the contained.'

Hero of Alexandria, Pneumatics I, p. 6, 11 Schmidt (p. 146, Paris edition): 'it should not be supposed, then, that among existing things there is some nature of void existing all together by itself, but rather scattered in small portions through air, through liquid, and through the other bodies — unless indeed one should say that adamant alone has no share in the nature of the void, because it admits neither burning nor cutting, but, when struck upon anvils and hammers, absorbs the blow entirely into itself. And this follows for it because of its continuous density; for the particles of fire, being coarser than the voids in the stone, do not penetrate into it, but only touch its outer surface; and so, not sinking in beforehand as they do with other bodies, it does not receive heat either. The particles of air, however, press against one another, but do not fit together at every point; rather there are certain empty intervals between them, just like the sand on the seashore. The grains of sand, then, should be thought of as corresponding to the particles of air, and the air between the grains of sand as corresponding to the voids between the particles of air; and so it happens that air, when some force is applied, is compressed and settles into the regions of the void, the bodies being pressed against one another contrary to nature; but, when the pressure is released, it is restored again to the same arrangement by the resilience of the bodies — just as happens with shavings of horn and with dry sponges, which, once compressed and then released, are restored again to the same space and give back the same bulk; and likewise too if, through some...

...force applied, the particles of air are separated from one another and a larger space, contrary to nature, becomes void, they run together toward one another again; for it happens that motion occurs quickly for bodies through the void, nothing resisting or pushing back, until the bodies press against one another.' Hero of Alexandria, Pneumatics I, p. 4, 2 Schmidt (p. 145, Paris edition): 'for some maintain that there is no void at all in the universe; others, that there is no void as a mass altogether according to nature, but that it is scattered in small portions through air, liquid, fire, and the other bodies, to which it is especially appropriate for it to be joined.' Simplicius, Corollary on Place, in the Commentary on Aristotle's Physics, p. 601, 19 Diels: 'of those who say that place is extended, some say it is extended in two dimensions, as Aristotle and the whole Peripatetic school do, others in three; and of these latter, some hold that it is altogether indifferent and can even remain without body, as the followers of Democritus and Epicurus do, others that it is an interval always possessing body and fitted to each thing, as the illustrious Platonists and Strato of Lampsacus do.' Simplicius, Corollary on Place, in the Commentary on Aristotle's Physics, p. 618, 20 Diels: 'others make it (namely the void) equal in measure to the body of the cosmos, and for this reason say that in its own nature it is void, but that it is always filled with bodies, and is contemplated as subsisting by itself only in thought, as many of the Platonist philosophers have held. And I think Strato of Lampsacus too held this opinion.'

Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's Physics IV 6, p. 652, 18 Diels: 'these, then, are the arguments Aristotle has set out of those who say the void exists. Strato of Lampsacus, however, reduced these four to two, namely to motion in respect of place and to the compression of bodies, and adds a third, from attraction. For it happens that a lodestone draws one piece of iron through another, when the stone attracts what comes out from the pores of the iron, by which body the iron is drawn along with it, and this piece in turn draws the next, and that one another, and so a chain of iron pieces hangs suspended from the stone.'

Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's Physics IV 7, p. 663, 2 Diels: 'these, then, are the arguments Aristotle has made in reply to those who posit the void because of these considerations. But Strato, resolving the argument from attraction too, says: "nor does attraction compel us to posit the void; for it is not even clear whether attraction exists at all" — since Plato himself seems to deny the existence of an attractive power — "nor, if attraction does exist, is it clear whether the stone attracts because of the void and not for some other reason. For those who argue this way do not demonstrate the void, but merely assume it."'

Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's Physics IV 7, p. 659, 20 Diels: 'and indeed it is only in these cases (namely, whatever keeps the same place as a whole) that the void will seem not to be the cause of motion in respect of place, since such things, taken as a whole, always remain in the same place. More apt, then, is...

...Strato's own example, which escapes these suspicions. For if someone, having thrown a pebble into a vessel filled with water, turns the vessel mouth-downward, holding back the outflow, the pebble is carried to the mouth of the vessel, the water changing places with it into the pebble's former place. And the same thing happens with swimming creatures too, both fish and anything else.' Hero of Alexandria, Pneumatics I, p. 16, 20 Schmidt (p. 149, Paris edition): 'if, however, it can be shown from visible, sense-perceptible things that void exists as a mass, occurring indeed against nature, while by nature it is void but scattered in fine portions, and that, through compression, bodies fill up the scattered voids, then those who put forward plausible arguments about these matters will no longer have any way in. For a sphere is constructed, of a sheet-metal thickness such that it is not easily crushed, holding about eight cotylae. Being sealed on every side, one must bore through it and insert a bronze siphon, that is, a thin tube, not touching the diametrically opposite point of the bored hole, so that there is a passage for water, the other part of it projecting outside the sphere by about three fingers' breadth; and the region of the hole through which the siphon is inserted must be sealed with tin, fastened both to the siphon and to the outer surface of the sphere, so that, whenever we wish to blow through the siphon with our mouth, the breath cannot in any way escape from the sphere. Let us, then, consider what follows.'

'For there being air within it, just as in all the other vessels called void, and the air filling up the whole of the space within it and pressing continuously against the container's boundary, and there being no void at all, as they suppose, in the place, we should be unable to admit either water or any other air, unless the air already present within it first withdrew. And if we perform the insertion with great force, the vessel will burst apart before it admits anything, being already full; for the particles of air cannot be contracted into a smaller bulk — for that they would need to have certain intervals within themselves, into which, once compressed, they might occupy a smaller volume; and this is not plausible if there is no void at all. Nor, if the bodies press against one another over their entire surfaces, and likewise against the container's boundary, could they, when pushed, make any place at all, there being no void; so that in no way could anything from outside be admitted into the sphere, unless some part of the air already present in it withdrew, if indeed the whole place is compact and continuous throughout, as they suppose. And yet, if one is willing to take the siphon to one's mouth and blow into the sphere, a great deal of breath will be admitted, without the pre-existing air withdrawing. And since this always happens, it is clearly shown that a contraction occurs of the bodies present in the sphere, into the interspersed...

...voids. This contraction, however, occurs against nature, on account of the force of the insertion. If, then, one blows into the sphere and, bringing the hand quickly to the very mouth, plugs the siphon with a finger, the air will remain compressed within the sphere for the whole time; but if one unplugs it, the air that had been forced in will again rush outward, with a noise and much roaring, because it is driven out — just as we proposed — according to the expansion, occurring by its own resilience, of the pre-existing air.' 65a.1 Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's Physics IV 9, p. 693, 10 Diels: 'these, then, are the arguments Aristotle arranged concerning the void. Strato of Lampsacus, however, attempts to show that there is a void running through the whole body, so that it is not continuous, saying this: light could not pass through water, or air, or any other body, nor could heat, nor any other bodily power. For how could the sun's rays pass through to the bottom of a vessel? For if the liquid had no pores, but the rays forced it apart by violence, it would follow that vessels full of liquid would overflow, and it would not be the case that some rays are bent back toward the upper region while others pass through downward.' 65b.1 Hero of Alexandria, Pneumatics I, p. 24, 20 Schmidt (p. 151, Paris edition): 'that voids exist, one might also grasp from the following. For if they did not exist, light could not pass through water, or through air, or through any other body at all, nor could heat, nor any other bodily power...

...for how could the sun's rays pass through the water to the bottom of the vessel? For if the liquid had no pores, but the rays forced the water apart by violence, it would follow that vessels full of it would overflow — which does not appear to happen. And it is also clear from this further point: if the rays forced the water apart by violence, it would not be the case that some rays are bent back toward the upper region while others pass through downward as well. As it is, however, as many rays as strike against the particles of the water are bent back, as though repelled, toward the upper region; while those that fall into the voids of the water, striking against few particles, pass on through to the bottom of the vessel.' Hero of Alexandria, Pneumatics I, p. 26, 13 Schmidt (p. 152, Paris edition): 'it is also clear from this that there are voids present in water, from the fact that wine poured into water is seen to diffuse and spread into every part of the water. This could not happen if there were no voids in the water. And light too passes through other light; for when several lamps are lit, everything is lit more brightly, the rays passing every way through one another. [But indeed light also passes through bronze and iron and all other bodies, just as also happens in the case of the sea torpedo-fish.]' Hero of Alexandria, Pneumatics I, p. 10, 9 Schmidt (p. 147, Paris edition): 'for fire, thrown into them (namely into cupping-vessels), destroys and rarefies the air trapped within them, just as it does with other bodies too...

...that are destroyed by fire and changed into finer substances, namely water and air and earth. That it is indeed destroyed is clear from the coals that remain; for these, though they preserve the same bulk as at the start before undergoing combustion, or a slightly smaller one, differ greatly in weight from what they were at the start.' Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's Physics IV 11, p. 711, 9 Diels: 'Strato of Lampsacus says that motion is continuous not only in virtue of magnitude, but also in virtue of itself, so that, if it were cut, it would be interrupted by a state of rest, and the interval between two states of rest is an uninterrupted motion. And motion, he says, is also a kind of quantity, divisible into parts that are themselves always divisible.' Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's Physics IV 11, p. 711, 35 Diels: 'but whereas Aristotle seems to have approached the matter from the clearer side, Strato, out of love of the elegant point, showed that motion itself, taken by itself, has continuity; perhaps also with this end in view, that the argument should be drawn together not only in the case of motion in respect of place, but in the case of all the other kinds of motion as well.' Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's Physics V 1, p. 807, 3 Diels: 'and rightly, I think, Strato says that motion exists not only in the thing moved, but also in that from which and that to which it moves, though in a different manner in each: for the substrate, he says, is moved as undergoing change, while that from which and that to which are moved the one as perishing, the other as coming to be.'

...Diels: 'since — the proof that this is so is that things moving according to nature move more quickly the nearer they come to their own proper places, few add — nothing perhaps prevents us from transcribing the proofs offered by Strato the natural philosopher on this point. For, in his work On Motion, having said this, that a moving body traverses the final change of place in the least time, he continues: this is clear in the case of things borne along through the air by their weight; for water flowing down from roof tiles, if one observes it falling from a high place, appears to flow continuously from above, but falls to the ground in scattered drops below. If, then, it did not always move more quickly through the latter part of its path, this would never happen to it. And he means by this that it is the part nearer the ground that becomes detached from the continuous stream. He adds, further, yet another proof, saying: if one lets fall a stone or something else having weight, releasing it from a height of about a finger's breadth above the ground, it will not produce any very noticeable impact on the ground; but if one releases it from a height of a plethron or more above, it will produce a powerful impact. And, he says, there is no other cause of the impact; for the weight is not greater, nor has the moving body itself become greater, nor is it pushing through a greater space, nor is it pushed by a greater force — it is simply moving faster. And it is because of this that this and many other such phenomena occur.' Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's Physics V 4, p. 965, 7 Diels: 'and Strato of Lampsacus too, who was a pupil of Theophrastus and is counted among...

...the best of the Peripatetics, agrees that the soul is moved, not only the irrational soul but the rational soul as well, calling its activities motions, including those of the soul. He says, then, in his work On Motion, among many other things, the following: for the one who thinks is always in motion, just as the one who sees and hears and smells; for thought is an activity of the intellect, just as sight is an activity of vision. And before this passage he has written: since, then, most of the motions are the same, both those by which the soul is moved of itself in thinking, and those by which it was previously moved by the senses. And this is clear; for whatever it has not seen before, it cannot think of — such as places, or harbours, or paintings, or statues, or men, or any other such things.' Simplicius, Corollary on Time, in the Commentary on Aristotle's Physics, p. 788, 36 Diels: 'Strato of Lampsacus, however, having found fault with the definition of time given by Aristotle and by Aristotle's followers, though himself a pupil of Theophrastus, who followed Aristotle in almost everything, took a more innovative path. For he does not accept that time is a number of motion, since number is a discrete quantity, while motion and time are continuous, and the continuous is not numerable. And if, because one part of motion is different from another, and of these one is prior and the other posterior, in this respect there is a kind of number of motion — then, on this reasoning, length too would be numerable (for this too is a quantity, one part different from another), and so too would...

...the other things that occur by continuity, one part prior and another posterior, so that there would even be a time of time; and further, there is no coming-to-be or passing-away of number, even if the things numbered perish, whereas time both comes to be and perishes continuously. And it is necessary that all the parts of a number exist together (for if the three units did not exist, neither would the triad), but this is impossible for time; for then the earlier time and the later time would exist simultaneously. Further, the unit and the "now" would be the same thing, if time were indeed number; for time is composed of "nows," while number is composed of units.' Simplicius, Corollary on Time, in the Commentary on Aristotle's Physics, p. 789, 33 Diels: 'and, having argued against Aristotle's account on many other points as well, Strato himself posits that time is the quantity present in actions: for we say, he states, that we spend much time travelling abroad, sailing, campaigning, and warring, and little time likewise sitting and sleeping and doing nothing, and we call it much time or little. Of those actions whose quantity is great, we say much time; of those whose quantity is little, little time. For time is the quantity present in each of these things. And this is why some say the same person arrived slowly, others quickly, according to how the quantity involved appears to each. For we say a thing is quick when the quantity from the point where it began to that where it ceased is small, but what has occurred within it is much; and slow is the opposite, when the quantity within it is much, but what has been accomplished is little. For this reason, he says, quickness and slowness do not exist in rest...

...for every quantity is equal to its own amount, and is neither much in a small amount nor little in a large one. And for this reason, he says, we speak of more or less time, but we do not speak of quicker or slower time. For an action or a motion is quicker or slower, but the quantity within which the action occurs is not quicker or slower, but greater or less, just as time is too. Day and night, he says, and month and year, are not time, nor parts of time, but the one is illumination and shadow, the other the revolution of the moon and the sun; rather, time is the quantity within which these occur.' Simplicius, Corollary on Time, in the Commentary on Aristotle's Physics, p. 789, 15 Diels: 'and he (namely Strato) also raises this difficulty: why is time any more the number of the prior and posterior in motion than of the prior and posterior in rest? For in rest too there is likewise a prior and a posterior.' Stobaeus, Eclogae I 8, 40b (Aetius I 22, 4, p. 318 Diels): 'Strato (holds) that time is the quantity present in motion and in rest.' Sextus Empiricus, Against the Physicists II 177: 'and so Strato the natural philosopher, departing from this notion (namely what Aristotle teaches, Physics 219b2), said that time is a measure of all motion and of rest.' Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism III 137: 'Strato, or, as some say, Aristotle, (says that time is) a measure of motion and rest.' Sextus Empiricus, Against the Physicists II 228: 'Strato the natural philosopher, though others say Aristotle, (says that) time (is) a measure of motion and rest...

Simplicius, Corollary on Time, in the Commentary on Aristotle's Physics, p. 789, 25 Diels: 'and against the claim that things are said to be "in time," he (namely Strato) seems to raise a good objection: for if this is what being in time means — being contained by time — then, he says, it would clearly follow that none of the eternal things would be in time.'

Simplicius, Corollary on Time, in the Commentary on Aristotle's Physics, p. 790, 22: 'and for this reason, he says (namely Strato), we say all things are in time, because quantity accompanies everything, both what comes to be and what already is. But we say many things in the opposite way too: that the city is in turmoil, and the man is in fear and in pleasure, since these are within those states.'

Sextus Empiricus, Against the Physicists II 155: 'it remains, then, to consider whether something can move, given that some things are divided to infinity while others terminate in an indivisible. And indeed the followers of Strato the natural philosopher were carried along this way: for they supposed that times terminate in an indivisible, while bodies and places are divided to infinity, and that the moving thing moves, in an indivisible time, over the whole divisible interval all at once, and not part by part in succession.' 82,1.1 Damascius, Doubts and Solutions, 389, II p. 236 Ruelle: 'for time (he says) is composite, as Strato says, made up of parts that do not persist.'

Simplicius, Corollary on Time, in the Commentary on Aristotle's Physics, p. 800, 16 Diels: 'and from these solutions it is also possible to resolve Strato's difficulties concerning the non-existence of time.'
[no text preserved for this fragment in the source]

Stobaeus, Eclogae I 23, 1 (Aetius II 11, 4, p. 340 Diels): 'Parmenides, Heraclitus, Strato, and Zeno (held) that the heaven is fiery.' Stobaeus, Eclogae I 24, 3 (Aetius II 17, 2, p. 346 Diels): 'Strato too himself (held) that the stars are illuminated by the sun.' Aetius III 2, 4, p. 366 Diels: 'Strato (held that the comet is) the light of a star enclosed by a thick cloud, just as happens in the case of lanterns.' Stobaeus I 29, 1 (Aetius III 3, 15, p. 370 Diels): 'Strato (held) that, when the hot yields to the cold, whenever it happens to be forced out, such phenomena occur: a crashing sound produces thunder, light produces lightning, speed produces the thunderbolt, and, by the excess of the matter that each draws to itself, whirlwinds and typhoons — the whirlwind being hotter, the typhoon thicker.' Hero of Alexandria, Pneumatics I, p. 10, 17 Schmidt (p. 147, Paris edition): 'the corrupted parts of bodies pass, through the vapours, into a fiery substance, an airy one, and an earthy one; for the finer parts of the decay pass into the topmost region, where fire also is; the parts a little coarser than these, into the air; and the parts coarser still than these, having been carried up to some degree along with the ones mentioned, because of the continuous motion, pass down again into the lower region and join the earthy parts. Water, too, changes into air, being destroyed by fire; for the vapours that rise from heated cauldrons are nothing other than the rarefactions of the liquid, passing into air. That fire, then, dissolves and transforms everything coarser than itself is clear from this. And also from the...

...exhalations that rise from the earth, the coarser bodies are changed into finer substances; for dews are carried upward in no other way than by the rarefaction, through exhalation, of the water in the earth; and this exhalation comes about through a certain fiery substance, the sun being beneath the earth and heating the region there, this substance being, moreover, mostly of a sulphurous or bituminous nature, which, being heated further, produces the exhalation to a greater degree; and the hot springs found in the earth arise from this same cause. Of the dews, then, the finer parts change into air, while the coarser, having been carried up to some degree by the force of the exhalation, once this force has cooled with the sun's turning, are again carried down into the lower region. Winds, too, arise from a violent exhalation, the air being pushed outward and rarefied, and always setting in motion the air next to it and continuous with it; the motion of the air, however, does not occur at an equal speed in every place, but is more violent near the exhalation itself, and grows fainter the farther it is removed from the place where it was set in motion — just as also happens with weights borne upward. For these too move more quickly near the lower region, toward which the force that sends them is directed, and more slowly the higher up they go; and once the propelling force altogether ceases to accompany them, they are borne again to their natural place, that is, downward; and if the propelling force accompanied them at an equal speed throughout, they would never...

...come to a stop. As it is, however, since that force gradually diminishes and is, as it were, used up, the speed of their motion diminishes too. Parmenides of Elea (and) Xenophanes of Colophon (held such views); Plato says that the earth turns, wound about the axis stretched through the whole, as though on a pivot. And yet Aristotle too, and the Stoics, left the earth unmoved; but Strato the natural philosopher seems to have been the first to make use of the reasoning now proposed concerning the earth's immobility.

Strabo I 3, 4 (49): 'Eratosthenes says that what caused the most puzzlement was how, at two or three thousand stades from the sea, in the interior, shells, oysters, and quantities of scallops and cockles are seen in many places, and salt marshes too — just as, he says, is the case around the sanctuary of Ammon and along the road leading to it, three thousand stades long; for there is a great deposit of oysters there, and salt too is even now still found in quantity, and blowholes of the sea throw up jets to a great height. In addition to this, wrecked hulls of sea-going ships are also to be seen, which the people there said had been cast up through the chasm, and dolphins set up on small pillars bearing an inscription reading "of the theōroi of Cyrene." Having said this, he (namely Eratosthenes) praises the opinion of Strato the natural philosopher, and also that of Xanthus the Lydian — Xanthus saying, among other things..., while Strato goes still further in laying hold of the cause, saying that he supposes the Black Sea (Pontus Euxinus) did not formerly have its mouth at Byzantium, but that the rivers...

...forced their way through and opened a channel there, and then the water flowed out into the Propontis and the Hellespont. And the same thing happened also in the case of our own sea (the Mediterranean); for here too the channel at the Pillars (of Heracles) burst open, once the sea had been filled by the rivers, and, at the outflow, the shallow places that had previously been exposed were uncovered. And he gives as cause, first, that the floor of the outer sea and of the inner sea is different, and, second, that even now a certain submerged ridge still stretches from Europe to Libya, as though the inner and outer seas had not previously been one; and that the region around the Black Sea (Pontus) is the shallowest, while the Cretan, Sicilian, and Sardinian seas are very deep. For, since the largest and most numerous rivers flow from the north and the east, those seas become filled with silt, while the others remain deep. For this reason too the Black Sea is the freshest, and the outflows occur toward whatever regions the sea-floors slope. And it seems likely that the whole Black Sea will in time be silted up entirely, if the inflowing rivers continue in this way; for indeed already now the areas on the left side of the Black Sea are becoming shallow marshland — Salmydessus, and the region called by sailors 'the Breasts,' near the Danube (Ister) and the Scythian wilderness. Against Strato, however, it might be said that, though there are many causes, he passes over these and attributes it to causes that do not exist. For he states as his first cause that the floor and depth of the inner and outer seas are not the same. But he (namely Strato) assumes this...

...believing that what happens in the case of rivers also occurs in the case of the sea, namely that the flow proceeds from the higher regions. For otherwise he would not have attributed the current at Byzantium to the sea-floor, saying that the floor of the Euxine (Black Sea) is higher than that of the Propontis and of the sea beyond it, while at the same time adding a cause: that the depth becomes filled and shallow by the silt carried down from the rivers, and that this is why it flows out toward the outer seas. And he transfers this same reasoning to our whole sea (the Mediterranean) in relation to the outer sea, as though this too were higher than the sea lying beneath the Atlantic; for this sea too is filled by many rivers, and receives the corresponding deposit of silt.' Plutarch, Epitome V 4 (Aetius V 4, 3, p. 418 Diels): 'Whether the seed is a body. Strato and Democritus (hold) that the power too is a body; for it is pneumatic (of the nature of breath).' Galen, On Seed II 5 (IV p. 629 Kühn): 'so that it would not seem unreasonable that Strato the natural philosopher supposed that the male animal comes to be through the predominance of the male seed, and the female through that of the female. In this way, indeed, he also thinks they differ by veins and arteries, just as they do by their generative parts, being without experience of precise anatomy.' Iamblichus (attributed), Theological Arithmetic 46, p. 62, 8 De Falco: 'Strato the Peripatetic, and Diocles of Carystus, and many other physicians besides, say that in the second week drops of blood appear on the aforesaid membrane, from its outer surface, and that in the third week they penetrate through...

...to the fluids, and in the fourth week, they say, the fluid coagulates and takes on, in the middle, something like a clot of flesh and blood — clearly having attained some completion, either because of the perfect nature of the number ten, or because of the combination present within it of the two odd cube numbers [bringing completion] — and in the fifth, or rather especially around the thirtieth and fifth day, the embryo is shaped in the middle of it, resembling a bee in size, yet distinct enough that head and neck and chest and limbs can be roughly made out within it. And this, they say, is fully formed in seven months; but if it is to be born in the ninth month, this stage occurs in the sixth week if it is female, and in the seventh week if it is male.' Plutarch, Epitome V 8, 2 (Aetius V 8, 2, p. 421 Diels): 'Strato (explains monstrous births) through addition, subtraction, displacement, or inflation (namely, that monstrous births occur through these).' Sextus Empiricus, Against the Logicians I 350: 'and some hold that it (namely thought) differs from the senses, as most do, while others hold that it is itself identical with the senses, as though peering out, as it were, through certain openings, the sense-organs — a position first held by Strato the natural philosopher and Aenesidemus.' Plutarch, Epitome IV 23, 3 (Aetius IV 23, 3, p. 415 Diels): 'Strato (holds) that both the affections of the soul and the sensations are constituted in the ruling faculty, not in the parts affected. For it is in this faculty that endurance resides, as in the case of terrible and painful things [and as in the case of the brave and the cowardly]. For some...

...attribute all of these together, taken collectively, to the soul, as Strato the natural philosopher does, saying that not only desires but griefs too, and not only fears and envies and malicious joy, but also toils and pleasures and pains, and in general every sensation, are constituted in the soul, and that all such things belong to the soul — since it is not our foot that hurts when we stub it, nor our head when we break it, nor our finger when we cut it; for the other parts are without sensation, except for the ruling faculty, toward which, when the blow is swiftly relayed, we call the sensation 'pain.' And just as we think the sound resounding in our very ears is outside us, reckoning into our sensation the distance from its starting-point to the ruling faculty, so likewise we think the pain from a wound is not where it received sensation, but where it had its origin, the soul being drawn to that point from which it suffered. This is why, when we stub our toe, we at once knit our brows, the ruling faculty quickly referring its sensation back to the part that was struck, and we sometimes even catch our breath; and if our limbs are bound tightly with cords, we press hard with our hands, checking the transmission of the affection, and squeezing the blow within the insensible parts, so that the pain does not reach the seat of consciousness. These, then, are Strato's views, on many such points, as is likely.' Plutarch, On the Cleverness of Animals III, 961a (cf. Porphyry, On Abstinence III 21): 'and yet there is an argument of Strato the natural philosopher...

...proving that there is no perception at all without thought; for indeed letters, when we run our eyes over them repeatedly, and words that fall upon our hearing, often escape our notice and slip past us, our mind being fixed on other things; then afterward it turns back and pursues and gathers up, gathering in retrospect each of the things that had gone unnoticed — whence the saying: it is the mind that sees and the mind that hears, and everything else is deaf and blind — since the affection occurring in the eyes and ears produces no sensation at all unless the thinking faculty is present.' Stobaeus, Eclogae I 52, 3 (Aetius IV 13, 7, p. 403 Diels): 'On Vision. Strato says that colours are carried from bodies, tinting the intervening air with their own colour.' Alexander of Aphrodisias, Commentary on Aristotle's On Sense 6, p. 126, 19 Wendland: 'whether, then, it is because the shape of sounds is altered as they are borne along, or because the intensity of the impact is relaxed, as Strato says (for he says that different sounds do not occur through the air taking on some shape, but through the unevenness of the impact) — in any case, however this comes about, that they are not heard in the same way as the motion itself occurs, and so on.' Sextus Empiricus, Against the Logicians II 12: 'and indeed the first opinion is championed by those of the Stoa (SVF II, fr. 166), who say that three things are linked together: the signified, the signifier, and the existing thing — of which the signifier is the utterance, such as the name 'Dion,' the signified is the thing itself made clear by it, which we apprehend as subsisting alongside our own thought, though barbarians do not grasp it even though they hear...

...the utterance, and the existing thing is the external object, such as Dion himself. Of these, two are bodies, namely the utterance and the existing thing, but one is incorporeal, namely the signified thing, and expressible, which becomes true or false. And this is not so of every case in common, but of one kind it is incomplete, of another complete in itself; and, of the complete, there is what is called the proposition, which they define, saying: a proposition is that which is true or false. Those associated with Epicurus and with Strato the natural philosopher, however, leaving only two — the signifier and the existing thing — appear to hold to the second position, and to leave truth and falsehood attached to the utterance itself.' Olympiodorus, Commentary on Plato's Phaedo (II 134, p. 174 Norvin): 'that, just as one attunement is sharper or duller than another, so too one soul is sharper or duller than another, so says Strato.' Theodoret, Cure of the Greek Maladies V 22: 'Strato, however, (said that the ruling faculty is located) between the eyebrows.' Plutarch, Epitome IV 5, 2 (Aetius IV 5, 2, p. 391 Diels): 'Strato (holds that the ruling faculty is located) between the eyebrows.' Pollux II 226: 'and mind and reasoning and the ruling faculty — whether it is seated around the brain, according to Pythagoras and Plato, or in the cerebellum or the membranes, as many physicians think, or in the space between the eyebrows, as Strato said, or around the blood, as Empedocles and Aristotle held, or around the heart, as the Stoa held.' Olympiodorus, Commentary on Plato's Phaedo D 63, p. 221...

...Norvin: 'Strato's difficulties concerning the first argument, the one from opposites. If existing things do not come from things that have perished, just as perished things come from things that exist, how is it reasonable to trust such an approach as sound? If a dead part is not brought back to life — as when a finger or an eye has been cut off — clearly the whole is not brought back to life either. Even granting that things that come to be from one another are the same only in kind, not in number. If flesh comes from nourishment, nourishment does not, however, come from flesh, nor does verdigris come from copper and charcoal from wood, in reverse. If old men come from the young, the reverse does not hold. If, while the substrate is preserved, opposites can come to be from one another, this does not hold once it has perished. If coming-to-be does not fail, even if it always occurs only according to kind, as is the case with artefacts too.' Olympiodorus, Commentary on Plato's Phaedo C II 178-190 Norvin: 'Three difficulties of Strato against the argument. Perhaps every living creature is in this way immortal, since it does not admit death; for there will be no living creature that has died, nor a soul that has died. In this way not even the composite will ever be dissolved; for it does not admit its opposite, since a composite thing, as long as it remains composite, will never be dissolved. If negation is said in many ways, the soul would be immortal, not as possessing unquenchable life or having unquenchable life, but only as capable of receiving one of two opposites, and being either with this or without it. Perhaps the souls of animals too are immortal in this way, insofar as they bring life and do not admit the opposite of what they bring. Perhaps the souls of plants too are immortal in the same way; for these too give life to bodies.'

'Perhaps every nature, too, is immortal in this way; for, providing what is according to nature, how could it admit what is against nature? And, not admitting this, it could never perish. Perhaps every coming-to-be, too, is imperishable; for it too does not admit its opposite, since nothing that is coming to be will be something that has perished. Perhaps this has been too readily assumed, that if a thing does not admit death, it is for this reason immortal in the sense of being indestructible; for a stone too is immortal in this sense, but not indestructible. How, then, does the soul differ, except that it brings life along with it, so that it does not admit the opposite of what it brings — for it is sometimes what brings it? Perhaps it is alive and has life as something brought in from outside, so that it can at some point lose it too. Perhaps it does not admit the death that is opposite to the life it brings, but admits another kind, opposite to the life that brings it. Perhaps, just as fire, as long as it exists, is unquenched, so too the soul, as long as it exists, is immortal; for it too brings life, as long as it exists. Perhaps, even if we escape all the other objections, we could not refute the claim that it is finite and has a finite power. For let it be granted that it both brings life and is separable in substance, and does not admit the death opposite to the life it brings; being, however, by itself, it will at some point grow weary and perish, being extinguished of itself, with nothing external coming upon it.' Olympiodorus, Commentary on Plato's Phaedo D 78, p. 226 Norvin (preceded by a syllogism about soul and death as mutually exclusive concepts): 'but even so, says Strato, not even the life present in a substrate admits its opposite. For it does not first remain and then admit death — just as coldness does not admit...

...heat. The life present in a substrate would then be as immortal as coldness is unheated — and yet it does perish. Further, he says, destruction is not the reception of death; for a living creature would not perish in this way either — for a living creature does not remain a living creature once it has received death, but, having lost its life, is dead; for death is the loss of life. These, then, are Strato's arguments... In addition to these points, Proclus says that for the soul to perish is to undergo death, and that undergoing death evidently means, as Strato himself says, that the substrate suffers the loss of life.' Olympiodorus, Commentary on Plato's Phaedo D 25, p. 211 Norvin: 'why does no one recollect anything without proof, as Strato raises as a difficulty?' Olympiodorus, Commentary on Plato's Phaedo II 41, p. 158 Norvin (cf. Plutarch, ed. Bernardakis VII, p. 31): 'that Strato raised the difficulty: if recollection exists, how is it that we do not become knowledgeable without proofs? And how has no one ever become a flute-player or a lyre-player without practice?' Olympiodorus, Commentary on Plato's Phaedo D 65, p. 223 Norvin: 'Strato's difficulties against the argument from recollection. Either souls possess their knowledge before time — in which case they are always knowledgeable, since they need nothing from time nor are affected by it in any way — or they possess it from a certain time, and then they know without recollection, as though learning for the first time; or else, at that time too, they recollect the knowledge that was present in them before entering the body — the poet, presumably, having made them perfect from the start, and so knowledgeable already. And yet, once they have come here, they need to learn; recollection is needed, then. Further, besides these points, Strato, in his...

...division, slips in some indefinite span of time; for between what exists before time and what exists at some point in time lies what always exists within time. Why, then, is recollection not ready to hand? Perhaps for some people recollection is indeed ready to hand, but for most it requires practice.'

Plutarch, Epitome V 24, 4 (Aetius V 24, 4, Diels p. 436): 'Strato (and) the Stoics (hold) that sleep comes about through a relaxation of the sentient breath, not through a loosening as though upon the earth, but as this breath is carried toward the ruling faculty between the eyebrows. And when the relaxation of the sentient breath becomes complete, death then occurs.'

Plutarch, Epitome V 2, 2 (Aetius V 2, 2, p. 416 Diels): 'Strato (holds) that, the irrational nature of thought during sleep becoming in a sense more perceptive, yet being moved, precisely because of this, in the domain of cognition (namely, that dreams thereby come about).'

Galen, History of Philosophy 106 (Diels, Doxographi Graeci p. 640): 'Strato: a certain other nature of thought during sleep, the soul becoming more perceptive, and, precisely because of this, becoming cognitive (namely, that dreams thereby come about).'
Stobaeus, Eclogae II 7, 4a: 'and, as Strato says, that which perfects the faculty by which we attain actuality (namely, this is the good).'

Clement, Stromateis I, chapter XVI, 77, 1 (cf. Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel X 6, 14): 'Scamon of Mytilene, then, and Theophrastus of Eresus, and Cydippus of Mantinea, and further Antiphanes and Aristodemus and Aristotle, and besides these Philostephanus, and also Strato the Peripatetic...

...recorded these things (namely the discoveries of barbarian peoples) in their works On Discoveries. And I have cited a few of them to establish the inventive and life-benefiting nature found among barbarian peoples, from whom the Greeks derived benefit for their own practices. The maxim 'nothing in excess,' some attribute to Chilon of Lacedaemon, as Critias does; others to Sodamus, as the inscription at Tegea shows: this is what Sodamus, son of Eperatus, who dedicated me, used to say: 'nothing in excess; all good things attend upon due measure.' Clement, Stromateis I, chapter XIV, 61, 1: 'again, on the other hand, some attribute the maxim "nothing in excess" to Chilon of Lacedaemon, while Strato, in his work On Discoveries, assigns the saying to Sodamus of Tegea.'
